Perhaps the most important difference between informal trial-type 
hearings and APA hearings is the type of presiding official. In an APA 
hearing, the presiding official typically is an Administrative Law Judge 
(ALJ) who enjoys various impartiahty and independence protections. (This 
is a newer title: ALJs used to be called “hearing examiners.”) By contrast, 
in informal trial-type hearings, the presiding official is a non-ALJ 
adjudicator. For example, immigration judges (IJs) are non-ALJ career 
attorneys subject to “supervision [who] shall perform such duties as the 
Attorney General shall prescribe.” 8 U.S.C. § 1101(b)(4). Issues related to 
the neutrahty, constitutional status, and management of presiding officials 
are addressed in subsection 3, below.
Although it is difficult to describe a “typical” agency hearing, the APA’s 
hearing provisions provide a basic roadmap of the key procedural elements. 
In practice, there is substantial deviation from the APA’s model, for two 
main reasons. First, as indicated above by the discussion of informal trial-
type hearings, there are hundreds of programs in which trial-type hearings 
are conducted “outside” (i.e., not in compliance with) the APA’s hearing 
provisions. For an examination of how Congress, courts, and agencies have 
contributed to this reahty, see Emily S. Bremer, The Exceptionalism Norm 
in Administrative Adjudication, 2019 WiS. L. Re v . 1351. Second, the APA 
estabhshes only minimum procedural requirements for formal hearings, 
which agency regulations embellish upon, sometimes quite substantially. 
Nonetheless, the APA offers a good place to start in understanding the 
basic elements of a formal hearing. Read 5 U.S.C. §§ 554, 556, & 557 and 
consider the following case.
